title: What Actually Transfers?
description:
Tell the deferred story of adding a second game system.

Narrative hook and core question: After building a deeply D&D-specific compiler, what parts of the architecture were actually reusable?

Do not draft or publish until Pathfinder implementation has materially tested the abstractions. Research source and license authority, source inventory, format-appropriate extraction boundaries, structural parsing versus semantic projection, shared semantic grammars, source-grounded executable curation, pack semantics versus engine services, system-specific versus shared engine behavior, tool integration, character-creation recipes, quality bars, freeze policy, and the lesson that reuse contracts, not document heuristics. The second system is the first honest test of abstraction.

Expected architectural conclusion: only Pathfinder evidence can show which contracts transfer and which apparent abstractions were D&D-shaped assumptions.

Boundary: do not write speculative architecture storytelling based only on D&D. Do not draft or publish before meaningful Pathfinder implementation and campaign-facing evidence exists.

This bead is intentionally deferred. Treat repository history, PRs, design docs, ADRs, audits, and playtest transcripts as evidence once Pathfinder work exists. Verify claims against artifacts rather than model memory; distinguish implemented architecture from planned architecture; preserve public readability and search indexing; and follow Joseph's voice rules: analytical and curious, concrete before abstraction, dry humor when earned, deliberate we/I attribution, reflect praise, absorb blame, no em dashes, and no generic LLM prose.
